# Computer memory (delay line, magnetic core, disc, semiconductor) (`computer_memory`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/computing.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Computing, control & information theory (`computing`)
- Deps: helped by binary_numbers, electromagnetism, vacuum_tube, sound_recording, semiconductors_transistor, integrated_circuit
- Core idea: A working memory holds instructions or data long enough to use them again. Capacity, access time and retention depend on the storage medium. Early answers were pulses of sound circulating in a tube of mercury and spots of charge on the screen of a cathode-ray tube, both slow or fickle. The reliable answer was the magnetic core: a ring of ferrite about a millimetre across, magnetised clockwise or anticlockwise, threaded on a grid of wires. A core flips only when both its row wire and its column wire carry half the switching current at once, so a thousand cores need about sixty wires, and the core keeps its state without power. For bulk storage, binary digits are written as magnetised spots on a rotating drum or disc or on tape. Later each digit becomes a tiny capacitor and transistor on a silicon chip.
- Pitfalls:
  - Giving every memory cell its own flip-flop of two valves; a useful memory then needs tens of thousands of valves
  - Forgetting that reading a core erases it, so every read must be followed by a rewrite
  - Core material without a sharp switching threshold, so that half-currents slowly disturb the stored digits
  - Assuming one kind of memory serves every purpose; fast small memory and slow large storage are always combined
- History: europe: 1932 – Tauschek's magnetic drum patent (Vienna); 1946–1948 Williams and Kilburn's cathode-ray tube store (Manchester); 1949 mercury delay lines in EDSAC (Cambridge); americas: 1944–1947 – Eckert's mercury delay line; 1949–1951 magnetic core memory (An Wang at Harvard, Forrester at MIT, Rajchman at RCA), in the Whirlwind computer from 1953; 1956 IBM's disc store (RAMAC); 1966–1968 Dennard's one-transistor memory cell; 1970 Intel's 1103 memory chip
- Read:
  - Emerson W. Pugh, Memories That Shaped an Industry: Decisions Leading to IBM System/360 (1984)
  - Martin Campbell-Kelly & William Aspray, Computer: A History of the Information Machine (1996)
